questions.q: Why is filling a trade at the next bar's CLOSE, rather than its OPEN, still an unrealistic assumption for a daily-bar backtest?
options: Close prices are never recorded accurately
It smuggles in a full extra day of price movement that the trader couldn't have captured, since the next bar's close isn't known until that bar ends
Open prices are always higher than close prices
There is no difference between filling at the open versus the close
questions.explain: Once a signal is known after bar N's close, the next bar's open is the first price actually quoted to the market. Filling at that next bar's close assumes knowledge of a price that hasn't occurred yet relative to when the order would realistically be placed.

questions.q: In the `limit_buy_fills` check `bar['low'] <= limit_price`, what is this function verifying?
options: That the signal fired on that bar
That the market actually traded at or below the limit price during the bar, rather than assuming the order filled simply because the strategy wanted to buy
That the bar's volume was above average
That the stock did not experience a stock split
questions.explain: A limit order should only be modeled as filled if the market's actual traded range during the bar crossed the limit price — not merely because the strategy's logic generated a buy signal.

questions.q: Why does conflating market-order fill logic with a strategy that was actually conceived as using limit orders (or vice versa) produce an invalid backtest?
options: Because market orders and limit orders always produce identical results
Because each order type has genuinely different, non-interchangeable fill conditions, and applying the wrong one means testing a strategy that doesn't actually match the one being evaluated
Because limit orders can never be backtested
Because market orders do not exist in real exchanges
questions.explain: Market orders fill immediately at the next available price; limit orders only fill if the market trades through the specified price. Using the wrong logic effectively tests a different strategy than the one intended.

questions.q: According to the fill-assumption checklist, what question mirrors the look-ahead bias check from Lesson 18, but applied to the execution layer specifically?
options: Does the strategy use a 10-day or 50-day moving average?
Would this fill logic survive being run live, bar by bar, with no knowledge of the future?
Is the strategy profitable before costs?
How many parameters does the strategy have?
questions.explain: Just as a signal must not use future information, the fill logic itself must be checkable using only information available up to that point in simulated time — the same no-foreknowledge principle applied to execution.

questions.q: What does this lesson say typically happens to a strategy's backtested performance once all five Chapter 4 realism checks (costs, impact, bias, overfitting, fills) are properly applied?
options: Performance typically improves, since realism always reveals hidden upside
Performance is usually unaffected either way
Performance typically gets worse, often substantially — which is not a flaw in the method, since a strategy surviving all five checks intact is one actually worth taking seriously
The backtest becomes impossible to run at all
questions.explain: Honest realism checks tend to erode a naive backtest's apparent edge rather than inflate it, because the naive version typically benefited from unrealistic, overly favorable simplifications — a strategy that holds up anyway is far more credible.
